name: Evaluation Protocols and Benchmarks for Learning Path Recommendation
venue: Protocol synthesis across KDD 2019, AIED 2020, CIKM 2021, AAAI 2023, CIKM 2023, KDD 2024, AAAI 2026, Scientific Data, Computers & Education, and public educational data repositories [uncertain]
url: https://doi.org/10.1145/3292500.3330922; https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v37i4.25630; https://doi.org/10.1145/3583780.3614897; https://doi.org/10.1145/3637528.3671947; https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v40i18.38591; https://github.com/THU-KEG/MOOCCubeX; https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.03072; https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2017.171; https://kdd.org/kdd-cup/view/kdd-cup-2010-student-performance-evaluation/Tasks; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9748379/
problem_setting: Design a reproducible, CCF-B-style evaluation protocol for learning path recommendation systems that recommend ordered concepts, exercises, courses, or resources under learner-state, prerequisite, difficulty, time, and learning-goal constraints. The protocol should support offline benchmark comparison, knowledge-tracing-based simulation, path-quality analysis, ablation studies, and a small controlled user study so that the method is evaluated as an educational intervention rather than only as a top-K recommender.
core_method: Use a three-layer protocol. First, build an offline benchmark layer with chronological user splits, graph/resource preprocessing, fixed candidate spaces, and leakage checks. Second, build a simulator layer in which a frozen knowledge tracing or cognitive diagnosis model estimates pre-path and post-path mastery, allowing every model to be evaluated on identical initial states, target concepts, path-length budgets, and action masks. Third, build a human-evidence layer with teacher blind review and a controlled learner study using pretest, assigned learning path, immediate posttest, delayed retention test, satisfaction survey, and behavior logs. Report primary educational outcomes, secondary recommender metrics, path validity metrics, efficiency metrics, robustness tests, statistical significance, and effect sizes.
data_sources: Recommended public datasets include ASSISTments 2009/2012/2017 for exercise correctness, skill tags, and knowledge tracing; KDD Cup 2010 Algebra and Bridge to Algebra for large-scale intelligent tutoring logs; Junyi Academy or KES-Junyi for math practice traces and concept relations where available [uncertain]; EdNet for large-scale hierarchical behavior sequences including question solving and other learning actions; MOOCCubeX for MOOC courses, videos, exercises, fine-grained concepts, concept-resource links, and prerequisite annotations in selected domains; OULAD for course-level VLE clicks, assessments, and dropout or completion outcomes; and project-internal AI-course logs from MySQL, Neo4j, and the assistant module. For this project, the strongest setup is to use MOOCCubeX or ASSISTments as external reproducibility benchmarks and the local Neo4j curriculum graph plus anonymized learner logs as an application benchmark.
evaluation_metrics: Primary metrics should include Learning Path Effectiveness or normalized learning gain, for example (post-path score minus pre-path score) divided by the remaining possible score; target mastery improvement; goal-achievement rate; learning steps or time to mastery; and delayed retention gain in user studies. Secondary recommender metrics should include Hit@K, Recall@K, NDCG@K, MAP, MRR, AUC, ACC, BCE, or RMSE when the task is reduced to next-item, next-concept, or knowledge-tracing prediction. Path-quality metrics should include prerequisite-violation rate, target coverage, path coherence, concept redundancy, review ratio, diversity, novelty, difficulty smoothness such as Diff-MAD, cognitive mismatch such as Cog-Gap, and explanation faithfulness to graph evidence. Report mean, standard deviation, 95 percent confidence interval, paired t-test or Wilcoxon test, bootstrap significance, effect size, and multiple-comparison correction.
baselines: The baseline suite should include Random, Popularity or MostPracticed, teacher-designed curriculum order, prerequisite-only BFS/DFS/topological path, shortest path or A* on the knowledge graph, user-based KNN, item-based KNN, matrix factorization or BPR, content-based recommendation, GRU4Rec, SASRec or another sequential recommender, BKT/DKT/SAKT/AKT mastery-gap heuristics, IRT or cognitive-diagnosis difficulty matching, graph random walk, LightGCN or GNN recommendation, contextual bandit, DQN, Actor-Critic, RLTutor, CSEAL, GEHRL, SRC, DLPR, and UNO/UniLPR when implementation or public code is available [uncertain]. For LLM-enhanced systems, include prompt-only planning, RAG planning without graph constraints, and KG-RAG planning with post-hoc validation.
strengths: This protocol aligns evaluation with the real objective of learning path optimization: measurable mastery improvement under pedagogical constraints. It avoids overclaiming from top-K accuracy alone, exposes whether paths are logically valid and difficulty-smooth, and separates model quality from simulator artifacts by using multiple datasets, multiple KT evaluators, and human review. It also gives a clear CCF-B experimental story: external reproducibility, internal deployment relevance, strong baselines, ablations, sensitivity analysis, statistical testing, and a bounded user study.
limitations: There is still no universally accepted public benchmark for learning path recommendation, and many public datasets were collected for knowledge tracing, performance prediction, or MOOC analytics rather than explicitly for path recommendation. Prerequisite graphs, concept tags, item difficulty, and learner goals are incomplete or inconsistent across datasets. KT-based simulators can bias evaluation toward methods that exploit the simulator's assumptions. User studies require consent, ethical review, careful randomization, and sufficient sample size, and short-term posttest gains may not reflect long-term retention or transfer. Cross-paper comparison remains fragile unless preprocessing, target sampling, path length, and action-space construction are fully released.
fit_for_current_project: Very high. The current project already has a Go recommendation backend, Vue frontend, Neo4j knowledge graph, MySQL learning records, and DeepSeek-powered assistant features. The protocol can be transferred by defining benchmark tasks over Neo4j concepts and resources, computing learner state from progress and quiz logs, creating fixed train/validation/test splits, implementing a baseline registry in the recommend module or a Python evaluation service, and using the assistant only for explanation and feedback collection. The most practical paper setting is a hybrid evaluation: public ASSISTments or MOOCCubeX reproduction plus an internal AI-course case study with teacher review.
implementation_complexity: Medium-high. A minimal protocol needs dataset adapters, concept ID normalization, chronological split generation, baseline implementations, metric computation, and reproducible configuration files. A research-grade protocol also needs KT or CDM simulator training, graph-quality checks, action masking, ablation automation, statistical testing, teacher-review tooling, anonymization, logging, and user-study management. The workload is manageable if staged as offline benchmark first, simulator benchmark second, and real learner study last.
paper_patent_value: High [uncertain]. For a CCF-B-style paper, the value lies in proposing a standardized evaluation protocol for graph- and KT-aware learning path recommendation, not only a new model. Strong publishable claims can focus on educational-outcome metrics, difficulty and prerequisite validity, simulator bias control, and teacher-plus-learner evaluation. Patent value is plausible around a closed-loop evaluation and deployment pipeline that combines knowledge graph constraints, learner-state simulation, path-quality auditing, and teacher-controlled safety rules, but patent novelty requires a dedicated prior-art search.
recommended_action: Create an evaluation harness before adding more recommendation algorithms. Step one: define a benchmark task schema with learner history, target concepts, candidate actions, prerequisite graph, resource metadata, and maximum path length. Step two: implement dataset adapters for local Neo4j/MySQL logs and one public dataset such as ASSISTments or MOOCCubeX. Step three: implement Random, teacher-order, prerequisite-shortest-path, KNN, GRU4Rec or SASRec, KT mastery-gap, contextual bandit, and graph-constrained reranker baselines. Step four: add metrics for learning gain, goal achievement, path length, prerequisite violations, Diff-MAD, Cog-Gap, Hit@K, NDCG@K, and teacher rating. Step five: run ablations removing KT state, graph mask, difficulty smoothing, similarity fallback, LLM explanation, and feedback-loop components. Step six: prepare a small controlled study with pretest, posttest, delayed test, satisfaction survey, and blind teacher review after the offline protocol is stable.
